title: Design a Search Ranking System
summary: A query-driven ranking case study, distinct from a feed's passive ranking — retrieval, query understanding, and click-bias-aware evaluation.

slides.markdown:
Search differs from a feed in one crucial way: there's an explicit **query** expressing intent, not just passive scrolling. This makes search naturally two problems chained together, not one model: **retrieval** — find the set of documents/products that could plausibly match this query at all — and **ranking** — order that set by relevance to the specific query and user.

A query for "waterproof hiking boots size 10" needs to first narrow a catalog of millions down to hundreds that are even topically relevant, before any ranking model spends compute deciding their order.

Before retrieval even runs, the raw query text needs interpretation:

- **Spell correction** — "waterprufe boots" → "waterproof boots".
- **Intent classification** — is this navigational ("nike.com"), informational ("how to waterproof boots"), or transactional ("buy waterproof boots")?
- **Query expansion** — adding synonyms or related terms ("sneakers" also matching "trainers") so retrieval doesn't miss relevant documents that happen to use different words.

Getting query understanding wrong compounds downstream — a misclassified intent or an uncorrected typo means retrieval searches for the wrong thing entirely, and no amount of good ranking afterward can fix that.

Retrieval typically blends two mechanisms:

- **Lexical retrieval** (inverted index + **BM25**) — fast, exact keyword matching with term-frequency weighting; excellent for precise terms (model numbers, exact names) but blind to synonyms or paraphrase.
- **Semantic/embedding-based retrieval** — embed the query and documents into the same vector space (see [retrieval-augmented-generation](retrieval-augmented-generation) for the same mechanism used in RAG) and retrieve by nearest neighbor; catches meaning-based matches lexical search misses ("sneakers" finding "trainers").

Most production search systems run both in parallel and merge the candidate sets, since each catches matches the other structurally can't.

Once retrieval returns a candidate set, a **learning-to-rank** model orders it — trained on features like query-document text match strength, document popularity/quality signals, and user personalization signals, optimized directly against a ranking-quality objective rather than a simple classification loss.

The query itself is a first-class feature here in a way it isn't for a feed: "best running shoes" and "cheap running shoes" should rank the *same* catalog completely differently, so query-document interaction features (not just document quality alone) are what drive most of the ranking model's value.

Search quality is measured with **NDCG** (rewards getting the top of the ranking right, see [evaluation-metrics-regression-ranking](evaluation-metrics-regression-ranking)), **human relevance judgments** (trained raters score query-document pairs on a relevance scale, providing ground truth that clicks alone can't), and **click models** (statistical models of how position and presentation affect click probability, used to interpret raw click logs correctly).

Human judgments matter specifically because click data alone is a biased and incomplete proxy for true relevance — which is exactly the pitfall below.

Raw click-through data has a built-in distortion: users click higher-ranked results more often **regardless of true relevance**, simply because they're seen first and scanned first. Training or evaluating a ranker on raw clicks without correcting for this reinforces whatever the current ranking already does — a mediocre result at position 1 can out-click a genuinely better result buried at position 8, purely from position, not quality.

The fix is explicitly modeling **position bias** (a click model estimates and factors out the probability a result was even seen) before trusting click data as a relevance signal, or relying on randomized result placement (interleaving experiments) to get unbiased comparisons.

slides.subTitle: BM25 scoring mechanics
slides.markdown:
**BM25** scores a document for a query by summing, over each query term, a weight based on how often that term appears in *this* document (term frequency) discounted by how common the term is across *all* documents (inverse document frequency), with a saturation curve so a term appearing 50 times doesn't score 50x higher than appearing once.

Concretely: the query "waterproof boots" scores a document highly if it contains "waterproof" and "boots" multiple times, more so if those terms are rare across the whole catalog (a specific technical term counts for more than "the" or "shoes"), with an added length-normalization term so a short, focused document isn't unfairly out-scored by a long one that merely repeats the term more.

slides.subTitle: Caching query understanding and retrieval results
slides.markdown:
Search has an advantage a feed doesn't: a meaningful fraction of queries **repeat** (head queries like "iphone case" get issued constantly), so query-understanding output (spell correction, intent classification, expansion terms) and even full retrieval result sets can be cached with a short TTL, skipping recomputation on a cache hit.

The long tail of rare, one-off queries won't benefit from this — which is exactly why systems still need the full understanding-plus-retrieval pipeline to run fast on a cold path, not just rely on caching to hide latency for the common case.

slides.subTitle: Overfitting ranking to head queries hurts the long tail
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Our overall click-through rate and NDCG look great, so the ranking model is working well."

**Why it's wrong:** aggregate metrics are dominated by high-volume head queries — a ranking model can look excellent in aggregate while quietly performing poorly on the long tail of rare, specific queries, since each individual rare query contributes almost nothing to the overall average. Users issuing those rare queries (often the most intent-specific, highest-value searches) can have a consistently bad experience invisible in the top-line number.

**Correct model:** slice evaluation metrics by query frequency (head/torso/tail) explicitly, not just in aggregate, since a model can win on average while regressing on a segment that never shows up in the overall metric.
